name: AdaptedMind
line: AdaptedMind places with a pretest and explains misses on video. In AMP, assessment and teaching come at every problem.
description: AMP vs AdaptedMind: AdaptedMind places with a pretest and explains a missed problem on video. In AMP, assessment and teaching come at every problem.
verdict: AdaptedMind places a student with a pretest, adjusts the difficulty as the student practices, and explains a missed problem in a teacher's video [1]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. AdaptedMind starts with a pretest that sets the starting point in its curriculum, and then an algorithm adjusts the difficulty as the student practices [1].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step and never the answer, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. AdaptedMind's grade picker sorts its math by grade, and lists grades 6 to 8 as lessons [4]. Practice is set inside a game, with points, badges and monsters [1]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [5].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After every answer, right or wrong, AMP shows the correct answer and the worked steps. In AdaptedMind the explanation comes with a missed problem: one of its teachers explains it in a video [1]. Across 40 studies of computer feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect [6].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. AdaptedMind's home page says it runs automatic assessments on new and old skills, and gives no schedule for them [1]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [7].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math and runs from counting through precalculus in one program, on one map of skills. A learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels, and repeated misses send practice back to what a skill builds on. AdaptedMind's home page calls it a K-6 curriculum [1], and its grade picker lists grades 1 to 8 [4].

rows.range: Its home page calls it a K-6 curriculum [1]. Its grade picker lists grades 1 to 8 [4].
rows.start: A pretest sets the starting point in the curriculum [1].
rows.teaching: When a problem is missed, one of its teachers explains it in a video [1].
rows.next: An algorithm finds each student's strengths and weaknesses and adjusts the difficulty [1].
rows.mastery: We found no mastery rule in the pages we read [1].
rows.review: Automatic assessments on new and old skills, per its home page. No schedule given [1].
rows.adult: A child works independently, by its account, and reports can go straight to a parent's email [1].
rows.reports: Real-time data and reports by email. Classroom reporting for teachers [1].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found on its home page, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][8][9].

theirs: AdaptedMind is an online math program its home page calls a K-6 curriculum [1]. It comes from GloWorld, LLC, a United States company founded in 2010, according to EdTech Impact [2]. The same company offers reading, science and social studies [3].

A student starts with a pretest that sets the starting point [1]. Practice is set inside a game, with points, badges and monsters, and an algorithm adjusts the difficulty as the student works [1]. When a problem is missed, one of AdaptedMind's teachers explains it in a video, and reports can go to a parent's email [1].
credit: A teacher's video explains a missed problem [1].
Placement from a pretest, then difficulty that adjusts as the student practices [1].

theirs: We found no outcome study of AdaptedMind on its home page, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][8][9].
ours: The two findings that bear most on this comparison: worked examples improve math performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 across 55 studies [5], and mixed, spaced practice scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks a month later, in a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations [7]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want a teacher on video to explain a problem your child misses.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate test.
You want a hint and a lesson at every problem, and the worked steps after every answer.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or ready for math past the elementary grades.
You want workbooks made from your child's own record, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: How is AMP different from AdaptedMind?
questions.answer: AdaptedMind places a student with a pretest and explains a missed problem in a teacher's video [1]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does AdaptedMind work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of AdaptedMind on its home page, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][8][9].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
